name: Carbon and graphite brush contacts
note: A soft, self-lubricating carbon block bearing on the commutator or slip ring under light spring pressure. Metal brushes weld and gouge; carbon wears the contact surface instead of cutting it, and its resistance limits sparking current at the moment of break. Baked lampblack or coke fired without air gives a usable brush; graphite is better and Rome has both. Every rotating machine with a commutator or slip ring needs this, and nothing in the tree makes it before now.

name: Laminated iron core
note: A solid iron core changing field builds up eddy currents that turn most of the input into heat instead of current or torque. Slice the core into thin sheets, varnish or shellac each face, and stack them so the eddy loops cannot close except across a thin insulated gap. Every dynamo, transformer and AC motor core needs this and the tree currently lets them all use a solid block for free.

name: Enamelled magnet wire
note: Silk-wrapped and oiled-linen wire, which is what copper_refining gives you, is fine for a telegraph line but far too fat to pack thousands of turns into a dynamo or transformer coil. Draw the wire fine, then pass it through a shellac or varnish bath and a sizing die repeatedly, baking a thin tough film on each pass. The insulation is now microns thick instead of a wrapped thread, and a coil that needed a barrel now fits in a hand. Without this a dynamo works but is the size of a house.

name: Glass to metal vacuum seal
note: A lead-in wire that carries current through the wall of an evacuated glass envelope must expand and contract with the glass across the whole firing and operating range or the seal cracks the moment it cools. Platinum happens to match soda-lime glass closely; a nickel-iron wire matches better and costs far less. Fuse the wire into the glass while both are hot, in the glassblower's flame, and check every seal by chilling it hard. Without a matched seal there is no way to get current into a vacuum tube at all.

name: Chemical getter
note: No pump reaches the vacuum a hot cathode needs; it only gets you started. Seal a pellet of red phosphorus or a magnesium strip inside the envelope, and once the tube is sealed off, flash it by induction heating from outside the glass. It vaporises, coats the inner wall, and chemically scavenges the last of the oxygen and nitrogen the pump could not touch, dropping the pressure by another order of magnitude or more. This is the difference between a tube that lasts an afternoon and one that lasts a year.

name: Exhaust and pinch-off technique
note: The assembled tube sits on a thin glass tail connected to the pump. Bake the whole envelope to drive off adsorbed gas from the internal metal parts while pumping, flash the getter, then heat the tail to softening with an oxy-hydrogen point flame and pinch it shut with tongs while it is still attached to the pump, sealing the vacuum inside as the glass fuses. Get the timing wrong and you either reopen the tube to air or leave a leak that will not show up for a week.

name: Controlled atmosphere furnace chamber
note: Molten germanium takes up oxygen and nitrogen from ordinary air instantly and ruins its own purity in seconds. Enclose the melt in a fused quartz vessel purged and continuously bled with hydrogen or an inert gas, with a rotary vacuum-tight gland where the pull rod or the induction coil's traveller has to pass through the wall while moving. The gland, not the gas supply, is the hard part: any leak past a moving seal undoes the whole purification programme upstream of it.

name: Seed-and-pull crystal grower
note: A chuck holding an oriented seed crystal is lowered to touch the melt surface, then withdrawn slowly while turning, so the melt freezes onto the seed one atomic layer at a time and copies its lattice. Pull too fast and the crystal thins and breaks free; too slow and it thickens uncontrollably; turn too fast and the melt surface distorts. The mechanism is a worm-geared rotation drive coupled to a lead-screw pull carriage with an independently adjustable rate, both needing the fine thread and steady motor speed that only now exist together.

name: Point contact whisker forming
note: Two springy phosphor bronze points are set onto the polished germanium surface a few hundredths of a millimetre apart, close enough that the depletion regions they create can interact. A bare point merely rectifies, like the galena detector; what makes it amplify is the forming pulse, a brief surge of current driven backward through each point after it is set, which locally heats and alloys a tiny puddle of the metal into the germanium and converts that point's contact from a simple barrier into one that can inject carriers. Point spacing and forming pulse energy are both found by trial on scrap slices before touching a slab you mean to keep.
